title: Three vows (ch. 58)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sick first: Benedict puts the care of the sick before all things. Your line was before all things. Did someone who is unwell get your time? Day one thousand two hundred two.

Don't make it easy to get in. That is roughly where chapter fifty-eight of Saint Benedict's Rule starts, on the subject of newcomers who ask to join. The one who asks is left waiting, and has to put up with a little rudeness at the door, to see if he means it. If he keeps asking, he's let in, first to the guest house, then to the place where the novices live. And during his time as a novice, the Rule itself is read aloud to him, more than once, with the same plain words each time: this is the law you want to serve under. If you can keep it, come in. If not, you are free to go. Today: the promise he makes at the end of all that.
screen: `ENTRY NOT MADE EASY.` → `THE RULE READ TO HIM, AGAIN.` → `IF YOU CAN KEEP IT, COME IN.`

segments.voice: When the time comes, the novice stands before the whole community in the oratory, the place of prayer, and makes a promise with three parts: stability, conversion of life, and obedience. Obedience had its own day earlier. Today is the first one, stability. Stability means binding yourself to one community, in one place, for life. A monk doesn't go looking for a better monastery when this one gets hard. He stays with these brothers, this abbot, this kitchen, this choir. In the Rule's first chapter, Benedict has sharp words for monks who wander from house to house, never settling anywhere. Stability is his answer to that restlessness. The second part, conversion of life, is harder to pin down. The Latin phrase is unusual, and readers argue over its exact sense. Some hear a promise to live the monastic way of life; others hear a promise to keep being changed, day after day. Then comes a small scene. The novice writes his promise out, in his own hand if he can, and lays it on the altar himself. And he sings a verse from the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Uphold me according to thy word, and I shall live: and let me not be confounded in my expectation." The community sings the verse back to him. Then he lies at each brother's feet and asks for their prayers. From that day, the Rule says, he's counted one of them. What stands out is that the first vow isn't about doing anything grand. It's about not leaving. The holiness Benedict has in mind grows in one patch of ground, among the same faces, year after year.
screen: `STABILITY, CONVERSION OF LIFE, OBEDIENCE.` · `STABILITY: ONE COMMUNITY, FOR LIFE.` · `THE PROMISE LAID ON THE ALTAR.` · then, large: `UPHOLD ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD, AND I SHALL LIVE.` · then: `THE FIRST VOW IS NOT LEAVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay with one commitment. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you've already said yes to: a person, a job, a project, a promise, a place. Notice whether part of you has been edging toward the door. Don't fix it. Just name it, and then, for these two minutes, stay. Sit still in this one spot, with nowhere else to be. If you pray, you can say the psalm line slowly: uphold me according to thy word. The bell holds the time.
Stability. The first of the three promises in Benedict's Rule: binding yourself to one community and one place, and staying. Today's word.
Your line: stay. Today, when you feel the itch to leave something half done, a task, a conversation, a chair, stay five minutes longer than you meant to. Day one thousand two hundred two.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns make their vows of stability, conversion of life and obedience during Mass or in the community's church, and the written promise is placed on the altar, as the Rule describes.

notes: The Rule is paraphrased throughout. Check the summary of ch. 58: entry not made easy; newcomer left to knock and bear harsh words; guest house, then novices' quarters; the Rule read to him repeatedly with 'here is the law… if you can keep it, enter; if not, freely depart'; promise of stability, conversatio morum and obedience in the oratory; written petition in his own hand laid on the altar; the Suscipe verse (Ps 118:116) sung and answered by the community; prostration at each brother's feet; counted as one of the community from that day. Specific counts in the Rule (days of knocking, months of reading, how often the verse is sung) were deliberately left out.
Ch. 1's criticism of wandering monks (gyrovagues) is summarized, not named. Confirm.
Conversatio morum: presented as debated, with two readings offered without ranking. Confirm the phrasing 'readers have long argued' is fair.
'Obedience we met a few days ago' refers to day 1192. howItsDone: confirm the description of profession practice.
